analogy.t: Monoclonal antibodies are like a lock‑and‑key system where every key (antibody) is cut to fit exactly one lock (epitope).
analogy.p: Just as a master key can open many doors, a polyclonal serum contains many different keys, whereas a monoclonal antibody is a single, precisely cut key that opens only one specific lock. The analogy breaks down because antibodies can also trigger downstream immune actions (calling the police), which a simple key does not do.

terms.d: Identical antibodies produced by one B‑cell clone that bind the same epitope.
A fused cell line of a specific B‑cell and a myeloma cell that can produce a single type of antibody indefinitely.
The specific part of an antigen that an antibody recognises and binds to.
Selective culture medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin and thymidine; only hybridoma cells survive.
Antibody with mouse variable region and human constant region.
Antibody where only the mouse CDRs are grafted onto a human framework.
Antibody whose entire protein sequence is of human origin, produced by phage display or transgenic mice.
Enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay used to detect the presence of antigen or antibody.
An engineered antibody that can bind two different antigens simultaneously.
Patient‑generated antibodies that neutralise a therapeutic monoclonal antibody, reducing its effectiveness.
Patient T‑cells genetically modified to express a chimeric antigen receptor derived from an antibody fragment.
The ability of a substance to provoke an immune response.
The constant region of an antibody that interacts with immune cells and determines half‑life.

mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies are made by injecting mice with the antigen and then collecting the serum.
mistakes.r: Monoclonal antibodies are produced in vitro from hybridoma cells; serum from immunised animals contains polyclonal antibodies.

mistakes.w: All monoclonal antibodies are fully human and have no side‑effects.
mistakes.r: Only fully human mAbs have minimal immunogenicity; murine and chimeric types can cause serum‑aspecific reactions.

mistakes.w: Hybridoma cells are made by fusing two mouse cells.
mistakes.r: Hybridomas are formed by fusing a mouse B‑cell with a myeloma (cancer) cell, not two normal mouse cells.

mistakes.w: Monoclonal antibodies can cross the blood‑brain barrier because they are small.
mistakes.r: mAbs are large (~150 kDa) and generally cannot cross the blood‑brain barrier without modification.

mistakes.w: ELISA uses monoclonal antibodies only as the detection reagent.
mistakes.r: ELISA can use either monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies; the key point is the specificity of the capture antibody.

mistakes.w: Bispecific antibodies are the same as normal monoclonal antibodies.
mistakes.r: Bispecific antibodies have two different antigen‑binding sites, whereas standard mAbs have identical sites.

mistakes.w: Hybridoma production does not need any selection medium.
mistakes.r: HAT medium is essential to select for hybrid cells; without it, unfused myeloma cells overgrow the culture.

exam.q: Explain how monoclonal antibodies are produced using hybridoma technology. (6 marks)
model: Immunise mouse with antigen – B‑cells produce specific antibodies (1)
Harvest spleen and isolate B‑cells (1)
Fuse B‑cells with myeloma cells using PEG (1)
Culture in HAT medium – only hybridomas survive (1)
Screen hybridomas for production of the desired antibody (1)
Clone positive hybridoma by limiting dilution and expand to produce mAb (1)
exam.tip: Use the verb ‘fuse’ and mention PEG; always state the purpose of HAT medium.

exam.q: List two advantages of using monoclonal antibodies over conventional drugs in cancer treatment. (4 marks)
model: High specificity – target only tumour cells, reducing damage to healthy tissue (2)
Standardised dose – identical antibodies give predictable pharmacokinetics (2)
exam.tip: Give a brief explanation for each advantage.

exam.q: Compare a murine monoclonal antibody with a fully human monoclonal antibody in terms of immunogenicity and clinical use. (8 marks)
model: Murine – 100 % mouse protein; high risk of patient developing anti‑mouse antibodies; can reduce efficacy and cause allergic reactions (4)
Fully human – human protein sequence; very low immunogenicity; can be given repeatedly with fewer side‑effects (4)
exam.tip: Structure your answer in two columns or paragraphs; allocate 4 marks to each type.

exam.q: Why are monoclonal antibodies useful in pregnancy tests? (2 marks)
model: They bind specifically to the hCG hormone in urine, giving a visible line when present.
exam.tip: Mention specificity and the target antigen (hCG).

exam.q: Describe one way monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat autoimmune disease. (4 marks)
model: An anti‑TNF‑α monoclonal antibody (e.g., infliximab) binds circulating TNF‑α, preventing it from triggering inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis (4).
exam.tip: State the target cytokine and the effect of neutralisation.

exam.q: State two limitations of monoclonal antibody therapy. (4 marks)
model: High production cost (2)
Large size prevents crossing the blood‑brain barrier (2)
exam.tip: Give a brief reason for each limitation.

exam.q: Explain how a bispecific monoclonal antibody works in cancer immunotherapy. (6 marks)
model: One arm binds CD3 on T‑cells, the other binds a tumour‑specific antigen (2)
Brings T‑cells into close contact with tumour cells (2)
Activates T‑cell cytotoxic response, leading to tumour cell death (2)
exam.tip: Use the terms ‘arm’, ‘CD3’, and ‘tumour antigen’.

exam.q: Outline the phases of clinical trials that a new monoclonal antibody must pass before being marketed. (8 marks)
model: Phase I – safety and dosage in small group (2)
Phase II – efficacy and side‑effects in patients with disease (2)
Phase III – large‑scale comparison with standard treatment (2)
Phase IV – post‑marketing surveillance for rare adverse effects (2)
exam.tip: Link each phase to the type of data collected.

exam.q: Give one example of a monoclonal antibody used to prevent infection and state its target. (2 marks)
model: Palivizumab – targets the F protein of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
exam.tip: Name the drug and the pathogen protein.

worked.q: A hybridoma line produces 50 mg of monoclonal antibody per litre of culture medium per day. If a laboratory needs 2 g of antibody for a clinical trial, how many litres of culture are required, assuming 100 % yield?
steps: Required amount = 2 g = 2000 mg
Production per litre = 50 mg
Litres needed = 2000 mg ÷ 50 mg L⁻¹ = 40 L

worked.q: Explain why a murine monoclonal antibody given repeatedly to a patient may become less effective over time.
steps: The mouse protein is recognised as foreign by the patient’s immune system.
Patient produces anti‑mouse antibodies (ADAs).
ADAs bind to the therapeutic mAb, neutralising it or accelerating clearance.
Result: reduced therapeutic effect and possible allergic reaction.
worked.ans: The patient’s immune response creates anti‑drug antibodies that neutralise the murine mAb, lowering its efficacy.

bio_ocra.15.9.summary: Cancer is a non‑communicable disease caused by uncontrolled cell division due to mutations in DNA that affect normal growth controls. These mutations can be inherited, caused by carcinogens, or arise spontaneously, leading to tumour formation, invasion of surrounding tissues and possible metastasis. Understanding the cell‑cycle checkpoints, oncogenes, tumour‑suppressor genes and the hallmarks of cancer explains why cancer cells proliferate unchecked and how treatments target these processes.

core.p: Cancer is defined as **uncontrolled cell growth** resulting from genetic changes that disrupt normal regulation of the cell cycle. The abnormal cells form a tumour, which may be benign (non‑invasive) or malignant (invasive and capable of metastasis).
bullets: Malignant tumour = cancer
Benign tumour = non‑cancerous, does not invade
Metastasis = spread of cancer cells to distant sites via blood or lymph

callouts.p: Uncontrolled cell growth caused by genetic mutations leading to malignant tumour formation.

core.p: The cell cycle is regulated by checkpoints that ensure DNA is correctly replicated and undamaged before division. Cancer cells bypass these checkpoints.
bullets: G1 checkpoint – checks cell size, nutrients, DNA damage
G2 checkpoint – checks DNA replication completeness
M checkpoint – ensures chromosomes are correctly attached to spindle

callouts.p: Loss of G1 checkpoint control is the most common cause of tumour formation.

core.p: Genes that control cell growth can become mutated. Oncogenes promote division; tumour‑suppressor genes inhibit division. Mutations that activate oncogenes or inactivate tumour‑suppressors lead to cancer.
bullets: Proto‑oncogene → oncogene (gain‑of‑function mutation)
p53, Rb are key tumour‑suppressor genes (loss‑of‑function mutation)
Both types of mutation are required for most cancers (multiple‑hit hypothesis)

callouts.p: Do not confuse oncogenes with tumour‑suppressor genes – they have opposite effects.

core.p: Cancer cells acquire capabilities that normal cells lack. These are the hallmarks that explain uncontrolled growth and spread.
bullets: Self‑sufficiency in growth signals
Insensitivity to anti‑growth signals
Evading apoptosis
Limitless replicative potential
Sustained angiogenesis
Tissue invasion and metastasis

callouts.p: All six hallmarks are required for a tumour to become malignant.

core.p: Carcinogens are agents that cause DNA damage leading to mutations. They can be physical, chemical or biological.
bullets: Physical: UV radiation, X‑rays (cause thymine dimers)
Chemical: tobacco smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), asbestos
Biological: Human papillomavirus (HPV), Hepatitis B & C viruses

callouts.p: Link each carcinogen to the type of DNA damage it causes – this is often asked.

core.p: Both inherited gene mutations and lifestyle choices influence cancer risk.
bullets: Inherited: BRCA1/2 mutations increase breast/ovarian cancer risk
Lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, high‑fat diet, obesity, lack of exercise
Environmental: exposure to radon, polluted air

callouts.p: Most cancers are caused by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental/lifestyle factors.

core.p: Benign tumours are encapsulated, grow slowly and do not spread. Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissue and can metastasise.
bullets: Benign: well‑defined, often removable, rarely fatal
Malignant: irregular borders, invade, can enter blood/lymph, cause organ failure

core.p: Metastasis occurs when cancer cells detach, enter circulation and colonise new tissue.
bullets: Invasion of basement membrane
Intravasation into blood/lymph vessels
Survival in circulation (avoid immune detection)
Extravasation into new tissue
Angiogenesis at secondary site

callouts.p: Do not confuse metastasis with local invasion – metastasis is distant spread.

core.p: Cancer is diagnosed using a combination of imaging, histology and molecular tests.
bullets: Biopsy – microscopic examination of cells (look for abnormal mitoses, pleomorphism)
Imaging – X‑ray, CT, MRI, PET scans to locate tumours
Tumour markers – e.g., PSA for prostate, CA‑125 for ovarian

callouts.p: Always mention at least two different diagnostic methods in an answer.

core.p: Therapies aim to stop cell division, induce apoptosis or remove the tumour.
bullets: Surgery – removal of solid tumours (effective for localized cancers)
Radiotherapy – damages DNA of rapidly dividing cells
Chemotherapy – drugs (e.g., cyclophosphamide) that inhibit DNA synthesis
Targeted therapy – monoclonal antibodies (e.g., trastuzumab) block growth‑factor receptors
Immunotherapy – checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab) re‑activate immune response

callouts.p: Higher‑tier exam may ask for the mechanism of action of a specific treatment.

analogy.t: Cancer as a runaway construction site
analogy.p: Imagine a city where building permits (cell‑cycle checkpoints) control when new houses (cells) can be built. In a normal city, inspectors stop any work that doesn't meet safety standards. In cancer, the inspectors are bribed or removed, so builders keep constructing houses without limits, eventually overcrowding the city and damaging existing structures. The analogy breaks down because, unlike a city, cancer cells can also send out workers (metastatic cells) to build new ‘neighbourhoods’ far away, and they can also change the landscape (angiogenesis) to suit their needs.

terms.d: A mutated form of a proto‑oncogene that promotes uncontrolled cell division.
A gene that normally inhibits cell division or promotes DNA repair; loss of function leads to cancer.
The spread of malignant cells from the primary tumour to distant sites via blood or lymph.
Formation of new blood vessels to supply nutrients to a tumour.
Programmed cell death; evasion of apoptosis is a hallmark of cancer.
An agent that causes DNA damage leading to mutations and cancer.
A non‑cancerous growth that is encapsulated and does not invade surrounding tissue.
A cancerous growth that invades surrounding tissue and can metastasise.
Genes where inherited mutations increase risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
A tumour‑suppressor protein that triggers DNA repair or apoptosis when damage is detected.
Drug treatment that kills rapidly dividing cells by interfering with DNA synthesis or function.
Treatment that blocks specific molecules involved in tumour growth, e.g., monoclonal antibodies.

mistakes.w: All cancers are caused by viruses
mistakes.r: Only some cancers have a viral cause; most are due to multiple factors.

mistakes.w: Benign tumours can metastasise
mistakes.r: Benign tumours do not invade or metastasise; only malignant tumours do.

mistakes.w: Oncogenes stop cell division
mistakes.r: Oncogenes promote cell division; tumour‑suppressor genes stop it.

mistakes.w: Radiotherapy works by killing all cells
mistakes.r: It primarily damages DNA of rapidly dividing cells, sparing most normal cells.

mistakes.w: Metastasis is the same as local invasion
mistakes.r: Metastasis is spread to distant sites; local invasion stays near the primary tumour.

mistakes.w: All tumour markers are diagnostic
mistakes.r: Tumour markers can be elevated in non‑cancerous conditions; they are not definitive alone.

mistakes.w: Chemotherapy only affects cancer cells
mistakes.r: Chemotherapy also affects normal rapidly dividing cells, causing side‑effects.

exam.q: Explain why mutations in the p53 tumour‑suppressor gene can lead to cancer. (2 marks)
model: p53 normally triggers DNA repair or apoptosis when damage is detected
Loss of p53 means damaged cells continue to divide, leading to uncontrolled growth
exam.tip: Mention both the normal role and the consequence of loss.

exam.q: Describe two ways in which a malignant tumour can spread from its original site. (4 marks)
model: Invasion of surrounding tissue (local spread) – tumour cells break through basement membrane
Metastasis via blood or lymph – cells enter circulation and form secondary tumours
exam.tip: Use correct terminology: invasion vs metastasis.

exam.q: List and briefly explain three hallmarks of cancer. (6 marks)
model: Self‑sufficiency in growth signals – tumour produces its own growth factors
Insensitivity to anti‑growth signals – ignores signals that normally stop division
Sustained angiogenesis – releases VEGF to grow new blood vessels
exam.tip: Give a concise explanation for each hallmark.

exam.q: A researcher discovers a mutation that makes a cell produce excess epidermal growth factor (EGF). Explain how this could contribute to cancer development. (4 marks)
model: EGF binds to its receptor and stimulates cell division
Too much EGF means continuous signalling → cells become self‑sufficient in growth signals → uncontrolled proliferation
exam.tip: Link excess ligand to the hallmark of self‑sufficiency.

exam.q: Compare the effects of chemotherapy and targeted therapy on cancer cells. (6 marks)
model: Chemotherapy damages DNA of all rapidly dividing cells, causing side‑effects
Targeted therapy blocks specific molecules (e.g., HER2) in cancer cells, sparing most normal cells
Thus chemotherapy is less selective, targeted therapy is more specific
exam.tip: Mention selectivity and side‑effects.

exam.q: Outline the steps involved in metastasis. (6 marks)
model: Cancer cells invade basement membrane
Enter blood or lymph vessels (intravasation)
Survive in circulation
Exit vessels at a new site (extravasation)
Form a secondary tumour
Induce angiogenesis at the new site
exam.tip: Give each step in order; use correct terms.

exam.q: Explain why smoking increases the risk of lung cancer. (4 marks)
model: Tobacco smoke contains carcinogenic chemicals that cause DNA mutations
Mutations in oncogenes/tumour‑suppressor genes lead to uncontrolled cell growth
exam.tip: Link carcinogen → DNA damage → mutation → cancer.

exam.q: Define a malignant tumour and give one example of a cancer that commonly metastasises. (2 marks)
model: A malignant tumour is a cancerous growth that invades surrounding tissue and can metastasise
Breast cancer commonly metastasises to bone, liver or lung
exam.tip: Include both definition and example.

exam.q: Why are tumour markers not sufficient on their own for a cancer diagnosis? (2 marks)
model: They can be elevated in non‑cancerous conditions
They are not specific to one type of cancer
exam.tip: Mention lack of specificity and false positives.

worked.q: A biopsy of a tumour shows cells with irregular nuclei, high nucleus‑to‑cytoplasm ratio and many mitotic figures. What does this indicate about the tumour?
steps: Identify the features described
Irregular nuclei and high N:C ratio indicate pleomorphism
Many mitoses show rapid division
These are characteristics of malignant tumours
Conclude the tumour is likely malignant
worked.ans: The tumour is malignant (cancerous) as it shows typical features of uncontrolled cell growth.

worked.q: Explain how a drug that blocks the HER2 receptor reduces breast cancer growth.
steps: State that HER2 is a growth‑factor receptor often over‑expressed in some breast cancers
Blocking HER2 prevents the receptor from receiving growth signals
Without the signal, the cancer cells cannot proliferate as rapidly
Result is reduced tumour growth and possible shrinkage
worked.ans: By preventing HER2‑mediated signalling, the drug stops the cancer cells from receiving growth signals, thereby inhibiting uncontrolled division.

bio_ocra.15.10.summary: Stem cells have the potential to treat many diseases because they can develop into specialised cells, but their use also raises safety, ethical and practical concerns. Understanding both the benefits (e.g., tissue repair, drug testing) and the risks (e.g., tumour formation, immune rejection, moral issues) is essential for evaluating stem‑cell therapies in modern medicine.

core.p: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can both **self‑renew** and **differentiate** into a range of specialised cell types. They are classified by their source and potency.
bullets: Embryonic stem cells (ESCs): derived from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst; pluripotent – can become any cell type of the body.
Adult (somatic) stem cells: found in specialised tissues (e.g., bone‑marrow, skin, gut); multipotent – limited to cell types of their tissue of origin.
Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs): adult cells re‑programmed to a pluripotent state using transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c‑Myc).

callouts.p: An unspecialised cell capable of self‑renewal and differentiation into specialised cell types.

core.h: Why stem cells are valuable in medicine
core.p: Their unique properties allow them to be used in several therapeutic and research applications.
bullets: **Regenerative medicine** – replace damaged tissue (e.g., heart muscle after myocardial infarction, dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson’s disease).
**Drug screening** – create patient‑specific cell lines to test drug toxicity and efficacy, reducing animal use.
**Disease modelling** – generate organoids that mimic human disease for studying pathology.
**Gene therapy vectors** – stem cells can be genetically modified and re‑implanted to correct inherited defects.

callouts.p: Stem cells can be expanded in vitro, providing a potentially unlimited supply of cells for therapy.

core.p: ESCs are the most versatile stem cells and offer several clinical advantages.
bullets: Pluripotent – can generate any cell type, useful for complex tissue engineering.
High proliferative capacity – can produce large numbers of cells quickly.
Potential to treat a wide range of conditions: spinal‑cord injury, diabetes (β‑cell replacement), macular degeneration.

core.p: Adult stem cells are already used in several approved therapies.
bullets: Reduced ethical concerns – taken from the patient (autologous) or donor tissue.
Lower risk of immune rejection when autologous.
Established clinical use: bone‑marrow transplants for leukaemia, peripheral blood stem‑cell transplants, skin grafts for burns.

core.h: Benefits of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)
core.p: iPSCs combine the pluripotency of ESCs with fewer ethical issues.
bullets: Patient‑specific – can model individual genetic diseases and test personalised drugs.
Avoids embryo destruction – created from adult skin or blood cells.
Potential for autologous cell therapy, reducing rejection.

core.p: Pluripotent cells can form tumours if undifferentiated cells remain after transplantation.
bullets: Teratomas contain tissues from all three germ layers; they are benign but can impair organ function.
Risk is higher with ESCs and iPSCs; strict purification protocols are required.
Regulatory bodies demand long‑term monitoring of patients.

callouts.p: Do NOT claim stem‑cell therapy is completely safe – tumour risk is a major concern.

core.p: Allogeneic stem‑cell transplants can trigger immune responses.
bullets: Host immune system may recognise donor cells as foreign → graft‑versus‑host disease (GVHD).
Matching HLA types reduces risk; immunosuppressive drugs are often required.
Autologous adult stem cells have minimal rejection risk.

core.p: Use of human embryos raises moral concerns and is heavily regulated.
bullets: Embryo destruction: many people consider it unethical; legislation varies (e.g., UK Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act).
Consent and donor rights must be documented.
Commercial exploitation: “stem‑cell tourism” can lead to unsafe, unregulated treatments.

callouts.p: Remember to mention the 14‑day rule for embryo research when answering exam questions.

core.p: Extended culture can cause chromosomal abnormalities.
bullets: Karyotype changes may lead to malignant transformation.
Quality‑control testing (karyotyping, SNP arrays) is mandatory before clinical use.

core.p: Stem‑cell therapies are governed by national and international bodies to ensure safety and ethical compliance.
bullets: UK: Human Tissue Authority (HTA) licences all stem‑cell research involving embryos.
EU Clinical Trials Regulation – requires Phase I‑III trials before marketing.
WHO guidelines (2021) on stem‑cell clinical use.

core.p: Real‑world applications illustrate both benefits and challenges.
bullets: Approved: Autologous haematopoietic stem‑cell transplant for leukaemia.
In trial: ESC‑derived retinal pigment epithelium for age‑related macular degeneration (improved vision in Phase II).
In trial: iPSC‑derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease (early safety data promising).

core.p: Stem‑cell research continues to expand, but a balanced assessment of benefit vs risk is essential for responsible medical use.
bullets: Potential to cure currently untreatable diseases vs. unknown long‑term effects.
Need for robust clinical trials, ethical oversight, and public engagement.
Integration with gene‑editing (CRISPR) may increase efficacy but also raises new safety questions.

analogy.t: Stem cells are like a master key
analogy.p: Imagine a master key that can open any door in a building – this is similar to pluripotent stem cells that can become any cell type. However, if the key is duplicated incorrectly (mutations) or used without permission (ethical concerns), it can cause security breaches (tumours) or legal trouble. The analogy breaks down because a key cannot grow or repair damaged doors, whereas stem cells can actually rebuild tissue.

terms.d: An unspecialised cell capable of self‑renewal and differentiation into specialised cell types.
Able to develop into any cell type of the three germ layers.
Able to develop into a limited range of cell types within a particular tissue.
The ability of a cell to divide and produce copies of itself without differentiating.
Process by which a stem cell becomes a specialised cell with a specific function.
Stem cell derived from the inner cell mass of a blastocyst; pluripotent.
Adult cell re‑programmed to a pluripotent state by introducing specific transcription factors.
A benign tumour containing tissue from all three germ layers, formed from undifferentiated pluripotent cells.
An immune reaction where transplanted donor immune cells attack the recipient’s tissues.
UK regulatory body that licences work involving human embryos and stem cells.
International guideline limiting in‑vitro culture of human embryos to 14 days post‑fertilisation.
Transplantation of cells taken from the same individual, reducing rejection risk.
Transplantation of cells from a genetically different donor.
Changes in chromosome number or structure that can occur during prolonged cell culture.
A 3‑D mini‑organ grown from stem cells that mimics the structure and function of a real organ.

mistakes.w: Stem cells are only used for treating cancers.
mistakes.r: Stem cells are used in regenerative medicine, drug testing, disease modelling and some cancers, but not exclusively for cancer treatment.

mistakes.w: All stem‑cell therapies are approved and safe.
mistakes.r: Only a few stem‑cell treatments are approved; most are experimental and carry risks such as tumour formation and immune rejection.

mistakes.w: iPSCs are the same as ESCs and have identical ethical issues.
mistakes.r: iPSCs avoid embryo destruction, so they have fewer ethical concerns than ESCs, though they share some safety risks.

mistakes.w: Adult stem cells can become any cell type.
mistakes.r: Adult stem cells are multipotent, limited to cell types of their tissue of origin.

mistakes.w: Teratomas are malignant cancers.
mistakes.r: Teratomas are usually benign tumours, though they can cause serious health problems if they grow in vital organs.

mistakes.w: The 14‑day rule applies to all stem‑cell research.
mistakes.r: The 14‑day rule specifically limits the culture of human embryos, not the culture of adult stem cells or iPSCs.

mistakes.w: Stem‑cell therapy never requires immunosuppression.
mistakes.r: Allogeneic stem‑cell transplants often need immunosuppressive drugs to prevent rejection and GVHD.

exam.q: Explain two benefits of using embryonic stem cells in medical treatment.
model: Pluripotent – can differentiate into any cell type, allowing treatment of many different diseases (e.g., Parkinson’s, diabetes).
High proliferative capacity – can produce large numbers of cells needed for therapy.
exam.tip: Give a specific example for each benefit to gain full marks.

exam.q: Describe two risks associated with the clinical use of pluripotent stem cells.
model: Risk of tumour formation (teratoma) if undifferentiated cells remain after transplantation.
Possible immune rejection if cells are not autologous, leading to graft‑versus‑host disease.
exam.tip: Mention that careful cell sorting and HLA‑matching are required to mitigate these risks.

exam.q: Compare adult stem cells with embryonic stem cells in terms of potency and ethical issues.
model: Potency: ESCs are pluripotent (can become any cell type); adult stem cells are multipotent (limited to their tissue).
Ethical issues: ESCs involve destruction of embryos → major ethical concerns and strict regulation; adult stem cells are taken from donors/patients → fewer ethical problems.
Both have safety concerns, but ESCs have higher tumour risk due to greater pluripotency.
exam.tip: Structure answer as a two‑column table in your mind – one column for each cell type.

exam.q: Outline the steps required before a new stem‑cell therapy can be used on patients (higher tier).
model: 1. In‑vitro testing – confirm differentiation into required cell type and check for genetic stability.
2. Pre‑clinical animal studies – assess safety, tumour risk and functional integration.
3. Phase I clinical trial – small group of patients, focus on safety and dosage.
4. Phase II trial – larger group, evaluate efficacy and side‑effects.
5. Phase III trial – multi‑centre, confirm effectiveness and monitor rare adverse events.
6. Regulatory approval – HTA/EMA/US FDA review of trial data and licensing.
exam.tip: Use the phrase ‘clinical trial phases’ – examiners look for the sequence.

exam.q: State two reasons why induced pluripotent stem cells are considered ethically preferable to embryonic stem cells.
model: They are derived from adult cells, avoiding destruction of embryos.
They can be patient‑specific, reducing the need for donor embryos.
exam.tip: Keep answer concise – each reason is one mark.

exam.q: Explain why autologous adult stem‑cell transplants have a lower risk of immune rejection than allogeneic transplants.
model: Autologous cells come from the same individual, so HLA antigens match exactly, preventing the host immune system from recognising them as foreign.
Allogeneic cells have different HLA types, triggering an immune response that may require immunosuppression.
exam.tip: Mention HLA matching explicitly.

exam.q: Give one example of a current clinical use of stem cells and describe the disease it treats.
model: Bone‑marrow (haematopoietic) stem‑cell transplant for leukaemia – replaces the patient’s diseased blood‑forming cells with healthy donor cells.
exam.tip: Choose a well‑known example; leukaemia is safe.

exam.q: What is the 14‑day rule and why is it important in stem‑cell research?
model: It limits the culture of human embryos to 14 days after fertilisation; it balances scientific benefit with ethical concerns about embryo development.
exam.tip: Link directly to ethical regulation.

exam.q: Identify two practical measures used to reduce the risk of tumour formation when using pluripotent stem cells therapeutically.
model: Differentiation protocols – ensure cells are fully differentiated before transplantation.
Cell‑sorting techniques (e.g., flow cytometry) – remove any undifferentiated cells.
Genetic screening – check for oncogene activation.
exam.tip: Any two of the three listed earn full marks.

worked.q: A researcher wants to produce 1 × 10⁹ dopaminergic neurons from iPSCs for a Parkinson’s trial. If each differentiation step yields a 70 % success rate and three sequential steps are required, how many iPSCs must the researcher start with?
steps: Required starting cells = required final cells ÷ overall success.

worked.q: During quality‑control, 5 % of cultured ESC colonies show chromosomal abnormalities. If a batch contains 200 colonies, how many are expected to be normal?
steps: Abnormal colonies = 5 % of 200 = 0.05 × 200 = 10.
Normal colonies = total – abnormal = 200 – 10 = 190.
worked.ans: 190 colonies are expected to be normal.

bio_ocra.15.2.summary: Plants defend themselves using layered physical barriers, chemical weapons, and coordinated signalling that can trigger localized cell death or systemic resistance. Detecting disease starts with visual symptoms, moves to microscopy and serological tests such as ELISA, and finishes with molecular methods like PCR or LAMP that identify the pathogen's DNA. Understanding each defence layer and diagnostic step allows accurate disease identification and targeted management, which is essential for high‑yield agriculture and ecosystem health. Mastery of the gene‑for‑gene concept, hormone cross‑talk (salicylic acid vs jasmonic acid), and the practical workflow from field observation to lab confirmation is required for top grades.

core.p: Plant pathogens reduce crop yield, quality, and food security; they also affect natural ecosystems. The specification expects you to link disease impact to the need for both innate defences and human detection methods.
bullets: Pathogens include fungi, bacteria, viruses, nematodes, and oomycetes.
Disease reduces photosynthesis, nutrient transport, and reproductive output.
Economic losses drive the development of resistant varieties and rapid diagnostics.

callouts.p: Questions often ask you to explain why a specific defence (e.g. cuticle) is effective against a named pathogen type.

core.h: 2. Physical barriers – first line of defence
core.p: The outermost structures block pathogen entry mechanically and chemically. They are constitutive (always present) and non‑specific.
bullets: Cuticle – waxy polymer (cutin) on epidermal outer wall; hydrophobic, limits spore germination.
Epidermal cell walls – thickened with cellulose, lignin, and silica; resist mechanical penetration.
Stomata – guard cells close in response to pathogen‑associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) via abscisic acid signalling.
Trichomes – hair‑like outgrowths that secrete antimicrobial compounds and impede insect vectors.
Lenticels and hydathodes – natural openings that can be sealed by suberin deposition.

callouts.p: A continuous, hydrophobic layer of cutin polymer embedded with waxes covering the outer epidermal surface of aerial plant organs.
Stomatal closure is an active, signalling‑dependent response, not just a passive barrier.

core.p: Plants store antimicrobial metabolites and synthesize new ones after pathogen detection. These chemicals can be toxic to the pathogen or signal to other cells.
bullets: Phytoanticipins – pre‑formed antimicrobials (e.g. saponins, glucosinolates) stored in vacuoles.
Phytoalexins – low‑molecular‑weight compounds synthesized de novo after infection (e.g. resveratrol in grape, camalexin in Arabidopsis).
Phenolics and lignin – reinforce cell walls, limit pathogen spread.
Pathogenesis‑related (PR) proteins – chitinases, glucanases, thaumatin‑like proteins that degrade pathogen cell walls.
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst – rapid oxidative burst damages pathogen membranes and acts as a signal.

callouts.p: A low‑molecular‑weight antimicrobial compound synthesized de novo by plants in response to pathogen attack.
Do not confuse phytoanticipins (pre‑formed) with phytoalexins (induced).

core.p: Local infection can prime the whole plant for faster, stronger responses. Two major pathways are Systemic Acquired Resistance (SAR) and Induced Systemic Resistance (ISR).
bullets: SAR – depends on salicylic acid (SA) accumulation; leads to PR gene expression throughout the plant; effective against biotrophic pathogens.
ISR – triggered by beneficial rhizobacteria; depends on jasmonic acid (JA) and ethylene (ET) signalling; effective against necrotrophs and insects.
Cross‑talk – SA and JA pathways often antagonise each other; the balance determines defence outcome.
Mobile signals – methyl salicylate, azelaic acid, and pipecolic acid travel via phloem to distant tissues.
Priming – pre‑treated plants show faster ROS burst, stronger callose deposition, and earlier PR gene activation on secondary challenge.

callouts.p: Questions may ask you to predict the outcome of SA‑JA antagonism when a plant is simultaneously attacked by a biotroph and a necrotroph.
A physiological state in which a plant responds more rapidly and/or strongly to a subsequent stress after an initial stimulus.

core.p: HR is a rapid, localized programmed cell death that restricts biotrophic pathogens. It is triggered when a plant resistance (R) protein recognises a specific pathogen effector (Avr) – the gene‑for‑gene model.
bullets: R proteins – mostly nucleotide‑binding leucine‑rich repeat (NLR) receptors; can be cytoplasmic or membrane‑bound.
Avr effectors – pathogen proteins delivered into host cells to suppress immunity; recognized directly or indirectly by R proteins.
Recognition triggers: ion fluxes, ROS burst, MAPK cascade, SA accumulation, and execution of cell death.
HR limits pathogen spread by killing host cells at infection site; also releases damage‑associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that amplify systemic signals.
Durability – pathogens can evolve new effectors to evade recognition, leading to resistance breakdown.

head: Component
Location
Function
rows: Virulence factor, recognised by R protein

callouts.p: For every resistance gene in the host there is a corresponding avirulence gene in the pathogen; recognition leads to incompatibility (resistance).
Do not state that HR works against all pathogens; it is mainly effective against biotrophs that require living host tissue.

core.p: Field diagnosis begins with observing macroscopic signs (pathogen structures) and symptoms (host responses). Accurate description uses standard terminology.
bullets: Signs – visible pathogen parts: mycelium, spores, fruiting bodies, bacterial ooze, viral inclusion bodies.
Symptoms – host reactions: necrosis, chlorosis, wilting, stunting, galls, mosaic patterns, damping‑off.
Distribution patterns – random, aggregated, edge‑focused, or systemic help narrow down pathogen group.
Host range and environmental context (humidity, temperature) are recorded for later lab confirmation.
Photographic records and GPS tagging improve surveillance and reporting.

callouts.p: Use 'sign' for pathogen structure, 'symptom' for host response; mixing them loses marks.
PAG B7 aseptic technique is used to culture fungi/bacteria from symptomatic tissue for confirmation.

core.p: Microscopy reveals pathogen morphology; culture on selective media allows isolation and further testing. Both are standard in plant pathology labs.
bullets: Light microscopy – hyphal septation, conidia shape, bacterial cell arrangement (rods, cocci).
Staining – lactophenol cotton blue for fungi; Gram stain for bacteria.
Selective media – e.g. PDA with antibiotics for fungi; King’s B for Pseudomonas.
Koch’s postulates – re‑isolate pathogen from inoculated healthy plant to confirm causality.
Limitations – obligate biotrophs (e.g. powdery mildews, rusts) cannot be cultured on artificial media.

callouts.p: A pathogen that can only grow and reproduce on living host tissue; cannot be cultured on artificial media.
Do not claim that all fungi can be cultured; rusts and powdery mildews are classic exceptions.

core.h: 8. Serological detection – ELISA and lateral flow
core.p: Antibody‑based tests detect pathogen proteins (antigens) in plant extracts. They are fast, relatively cheap, and suitable for high‑throughput screening.
bullets: Direct antigen coating (DAC‑ELISA) – plant sap coated, detection antibody added.
Double‑antibody sandwich (DAS‑ELISA) – capture antibody on plate, then antigen, then detection antibody‑enzyme conjugate.
Readout – colour change measured at 405 nm (pNPP substrate) or 650 nm (TMB).
Lateral flow devices (LFD) – handheld dipsticks for field use; give qualitative yes/no within minutes.
Sensitivity – typically 1–10 ng mL⁻¹; specificity depends on antibody quality; cross‑reactivity can give false positives.

callouts.p: ‘Antibody binds specifically to pathogen antigen; enzyme‑substrate reaction produces colour proportional to antigen amount.’
ELISA gives quantitative data (standard curve); LFD is usually qualitative.

core.h: 9. Molecular detection – PCR, qPCR, LAMP, sequencing
core.p: Nucleic‑acid‑based methods detect pathogen DNA/RNA with high specificity and sensitivity. They are the gold standard for certification and research.
bullets: Conventional PCR – endpoint detection on agarose gel; requires thermal cycler.
Real‑time qPCR – fluorescent probes (TaqMan) or intercalating dyes (SYBR Green); gives Ct values for quantification.
Loop‑mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) – single temperature (60–65 °C), visual colour change; field‑deployable.
DNA barcoding / amplicon sequencing – ITS region for fungi, 16S rRNA for bacteria, specific viral primers.
Next‑generation sequencing (NGS) – metagenomics for unknown pathogens; bioinformatics pipelines identify species.
Controls – positive, negative, no‑template, and internal plant gene (e.g. actin) to verify extraction quality.

callouts.p: Cycle threshold in qPCR; the cycle number at which fluorescence exceeds background; lower Ct = higher starting template quantity.
Do not confuse LAMP (isothermal) with PCR (thermal cycling); they use different polymerases and primer sets.

core.h: 10. Disease identification keys and digital tools
core.p: After detection, the pathogen must be identified to species or pathovar level. Dichotomous keys, multi‑access keys, and smartphone apps integrate morphological and molecular data.
bullets: Traditional dichotomous keys – stepwise couplets based on spore size, septation, host range.
Multi‑access (polyclave) keys – user selects any observable characters; software filters taxa.
Digital image recognition – AI models trained on symptom photos give provisional IDs.
Databases – EPPO Global Database, CABI Crop Protection Compendium, NCBI GenBank for sequence BLAST.
Reporting – positive IDs for quarantine pests must be reported to national plant protection organisations (NPPOs).

callouts.p: When asked to design a key, use clear, mutually exclusive couplets (e.g. ‘spores septate / spores aseptate’).
Quarantine pathogens (e.g. Xylella fastidiosa) require official diagnostic protocols (EPPO PM 7/XX).

core.h: 11. Practical skills – aseptic technique (PAG B7) for plant pathogens
core.p: Aseptic technique prevents contamination when isolating fungi or bacteria from diseased tissue. It is assessed in the required practical.
bullets: Flame sterilise loops/needles; work near Bunsen burner or in laminar flow hood.
Surface‑sterilise plant material (70 % ethanol 30 s, 1 % NaOCl 1–2 min, rinse sterile water).
Plate onto selective agar; seal with Parafilm; incubate at appropriate temperature (e.g. 22 °C for fungi, 28 °C for many bacteria).
Sub‑culture pure colonies; store as glycerol stocks at −80 °C.
Record colony morphology, growth rate, and microscopic features for identification.

callouts.p: A set of procedures that prevent unwanted microorganisms from contaminating cultures or samples.
Forgetting to cool the loop after flaming kills the pathogen you are trying to isolate.

core.h: 12. Exam technique – linking defence to detection
core.p: High‑mark questions require you to connect a defence mechanism to a diagnostic outcome (e.g. HR limits pathogen spread, so PCR from symptomatic tissue may give low template). Practice integrating concepts.
bullets: Use the phrase ‘because’ to explain causality (e.g. ‘SA accumulates because PRR recognises PAMP, leading to SAR’).
Quote specific molecules (SA, JA, ROS, PR‑1, NLR, Avr) – generic ‘hormone’ loses marks.
For detection questions, state the principle (antibody‑antigen binding, DNA amplification) and a limitation (cross‑reactivity, need for pure culture).
Structure 6‑mark answers: 1) definition, 2) mechanism, 3) example, 4) significance/limitation.
Time management: allocate ~1 min per mark; underline command words (describe, explain, compare).

callouts.p: ‘Describe’ = what you see; ‘Explain’ = why it happens; ‘Compare’ = similarities and differences in a table.
Always link back to the specification wording: ‘physical barrier’, ‘chemical defence’, ‘systemic acquired resistance’, ‘gene‑for‑gene’.

analogy.t: Plant immunity as a medieval castle
analogy.p: The cuticle and cell walls are the high stone walls and moat that stop most invaders at the border. Stomata are guarded gates that can be slammed shut when a scout (PAMP) is spotted. Inside, phytoanticipins are stored weapons in the armory, while phytoalexins are forged on‑demand by blacksmiths (enzymes) when the alarm sounds. The hypersensitive response is a controlled burning of a tower to deny the enemy a foothold, and systemic acquired resistance is the messenger pigeons carrying the warning to distant outposts so they raise their shields (PR proteins) before the attack arrives. Detection methods are the spies: visual scouts (symptoms), microscope spies (microscopy), antibody‑bearing messengers (ELISA), and DNA code‑breakers (PCR). The analogy breaks down because plants lack a central nervous system; signalling is chemical and hydraulic, not electrical, and the ‘castle’ can regrow damaged walls through meristems.

terms.d: A continuous, hydrophobic layer of cutin polymer embedded with waxes covering the outer epidermal surface of aerial plant organs.
A pre‑formed antimicrobial compound stored in plant cells that is active against pathogens before infection occurs.
A low‑molecular‑weight antimicrobial compound synthesized de novo by plants in response to pathogen attack.
A group of plant proteins (e.g. chitinases, glucanases) induced during pathogen infection that contribute to defence.
A long‑lasting, broad‑spectrum resistance activated throughout the plant after a localized infection, dependent on salicylic acid signalling.
A resistance state triggered by beneficial root‑colonising microbes, mediated by jasmonic acid and ethylene pathways.
Rapid, localized programmed cell death at the infection site that restricts biotrophic pathogen growth.
For each resistance (R) gene in the host there is a corresponding avirulence (Avr) gene in the pathogen; recognition leads to incompatibility.
A pathogen‑secreted protein that manipulates host physiology; recognised by host R proteins to trigger immunity.
A phenolic hormone central to SAR signalling; accumulates after biotrophic infection and activates PR genes.
An oxylipin hormone that mediates defence against necrotrophs and herbivores, often antagonistic to SA.
A rapid, transient production of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide at the infection site, acting as both antimicrobial agent and signalling molecule.
A serological test that uses antibodies to detect specific pathogen antigens, producing a colour change proportional to antigen amount.
A molecular technique that amplifies a specific DNA sequence through repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension.
PCR monitored in real time via fluorescence; the cycle threshold (Ct) quantifies initial template copy number.
An isothermal nucleic‑acid amplification method using a strand‑displacing polymerase and multiple primers, giving a visual colour change.
A set of criteria to establish a causative relationship between a microorganism and a disease: isolate, culture, inoculate, re‑isolate.

mistakes.w: Phytoanticipins are produced after infection.
mistakes.r: Phytoanticipins are pre‑formed; phytoalexins are induced after infection.

mistakes.w: HR works against all pathogens.
mistakes.r: HR is mainly effective against biotrophic pathogens that require living host tissue.

mistakes.w: SA and JA pathways always work together.
mistakes.r: SA and JA pathways are often antagonistic; cross‑talk determines defence outcome.

mistakes.w: ELISA detects pathogen DNA.
mistakes.r: ELISA detects pathogen proteins (antigens) using antibodies; PCR detects DNA.

mistakes.w: All fungi can be cultured on PDA.
mistakes.r: Obligate biotrophs (e.g. powdery mildews, rusts) cannot grow on artificial media.

mistakes.w: LAMP requires a thermal cycler.
mistakes.r: LAMP is isothermal (single temperature) and only needs a water bath or heating block.

mistakes.w: A positive ELISA result always means active disease.
mistakes.r: ELISA can detect dead pathogen debris; confirm with culture or PCR for viability.

mistakes.w: Systemic acquired resistance is induced by rhizobacteria.
mistakes.r: SAR is induced by pathogen infection (SA‑dependent); ISR is induced by beneficial rhizobacteria (JA/ET‑dependent).

mistakes.w: The gene‑for‑gene model applies to all plant‑pathogen interactions.
mistakes.r: Gene‑for‑gene applies specifically to interactions where a single R gene recognises a single Avr effector; many interactions are quantitative.

mistakes.w: Ct value increases with more template.
mistakes.r: Ct value decreases as starting template quantity increases (inverse relationship).

exam.q: Describe two physical barriers that prevent pathogen entry into a leaf.
model: Cuticle – waxy hydrophobic layer that blocks fungal spore germination.
Epidermal cell walls thickened with lignin/silica that resist mechanical penetration.
exam.tip: Name the barrier and state its composition/function.

exam.q: Explain how the hypersensitive response limits the spread of a biotrophic fungus.
model: HR triggers rapid programmed cell death of the infected host cell.
Dead cells deprive the biotroph of living tissue it needs for nutrition.
Cell death releases DAMPs that amplify systemic signalling (e.g. SA).
Surrounding cells deposit callose and lignin, reinforcing the barrier.
exam.tip: Link cell death to biotroph requirement for living host.

exam.q: Compare Systemic Acquired Resistance (SAR) and Induced Systemic Resistance (ISR) in a table.
model: SAR: induced by pathogen infection; SA‑dependent; effective vs biotrophs; marker PR‑1.
ISR: induced by beneficial rhizobacteria; JA/ET‑dependent; effective vs necrotrophs/insects; marker PDF1.2.
Both provide broad‑spectrum, long‑lasting resistance throughout the plant.
Antagonism between SA and JA pathways can modulate the balance.
exam.tip: Use a clear table with at least three comparison rows.

exam.q: A farmer observes yellow mosaic patterns on tomato leaves. Outline the steps to identify the causal virus using laboratory methods.
model: 1. Record symptoms and collect symptomatic leaf tissue aseptically.
2. Perform mechanical inoculation onto indicator plants to confirm infectivity.
3. Extract total RNA from infected tissue.
4. Run RT‑PCR with virus‑specific primers (e.g. for TMV, ToMV).
5. Visualise amplicon on agarose gel; sequence product for confirmation.
6. Compare sequence to GenBank via BLAST to assign virus species.
exam.tip: Include both biological (indicator plants) and molecular steps.

exam.q: State the principle of a double‑antibody sandwich ELISA (DAS‑ELISA) for detecting a plant virus.
model: Capture antibody coated on the plate binds the virus antigen from plant sap.
Detection antibody‑enzyme conjugate binds a different epitope on the same virus particle.
Substrate conversion produces colour proportional to virus concentration.
exam.tip: Mention two antibodies binding different epitopes.

exam.q: Why can obligate biotrophic fungi such as powdery mildew not be cultured on standard agar media?
model: They require living host cells to obtain nutrients and complete their life cycle.
Artificial media lack the specific host signals and living cytoplasm they depend on.
exam.tip: Use the term ‘obligate biotroph’.

exam.q: Describe how salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA) interact to regulate defence against a biotroph and a necrotroph simultaneously attacking a plant.
model: SA pathway activated by biotroph leads to SAR and PR gene expression.
JA pathway activated by necrotroph leads to ISR and anti‑herbivore defences.
SA and JA signalling are mutually antagonistic; high SA suppresses JA responses.
Result: plant may prioritise defence against the biotroph, becoming more susceptible to the necrotroph.
exam.tip: Explain antagonism and trade‑off.

exam.q: A qPCR assay for Xylella fastidiosa gives a Ct of 22 for a sample and a Ct of 28 for a negative control. Interpret these results.
model: Ct 22 indicates a high amount of target DNA – positive detection of X. fastidiosa.
Ct 28 in negative control suggests low‑level contamination or primer‑dimer; should be >35 or undetermined for a true negative.
exam.tip: Lower Ct = more template; negative control should be very high/undetermined.

exam.q: Design a dichotomous key couplet to separate two fungal genera: one produces septate hyphae and conidia in chains, the other produces aseptate hyphae and sporangia.
model: 1a. Hyphae septate … go to genus A (e.g. Aspergillus).
1b. Hyphae aseptate … go to genus B (e.g. Rhizopus).
exam.tip: Use mutually exclusive, observable characters.

exam.q: Explain why aseptic technique is essential when isolating a bacterium from a leaf lesion for Koch’s postulates.
model: Prevents contaminant microbes from overgrowing the target pathogen.
Ensures the isolated colony originates from the lesion, fulfilling the ‘pure culture’ requirement.
exam.tip: Mention pure culture and contamination risk.

exam.q: A lateral flow device (LFD) for Phytophthora infestans shows a faint test line. What does this indicate and what should the grower do next?
model: Faint line = low antigen concentration; likely early infection or low pathogen load.
Grower should confirm with a more sensitive method (e.g. qPCR) and consider preventive fungicide application.
exam.tip: Link sensitivity to next diagnostic step.

worked.q: A researcher runs a DAS‑ELISA for Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) and obtains absorbance values: blank 0.05, negative control 0.07, sample 0.42, positive control 0.85. The cut‑off is defined as mean negative + 3 SD (SD = 0.01). Determine if the sample is positive.
steps: Calculate cut‑off: mean negative = 0.07; 3 SD = 0.03; cut‑off = 0.10.
Compare sample absorbance (0.42) to cut‑off (0.10).
0.42 > 0.10, therefore sample is positive for CMV.
worked.ans: Positive – sample absorbance exceeds the calculated cut‑off.

worked.q: A qPCR for Potato virus Y (PVY) yields Ct values: standard curve points (log10 copies, Ct) = (6, 15), (5, 18), (4, 21), (3, 24). An unknown sample gives Ct = 20. Estimate the viral copy number in the reaction.
steps: Determine slope: (24‑15)/(3‑6) = 9/‑3 = ‑3.0 Ct per log10 copy.
Equation: Ct = ‑3.0 × log10(copies) + intercept. Use point (6,15): 15 = ‑3 × 6 + b → b = 33.
Plug Ct = 20: 20 = ‑3 × log10(copies) + 33 → ‑3 × log10(copies) = ‑13 → log10(copies) = 4.33.
Copies = 10^4.33 ≈ 2.1 × 10^4 copies per reaction.
worked.ans: Approximately 2 × 10^4 PVY RNA copies per reaction.

worked.q: A student designs a LAMP assay for detecting Fusarium oxysporum. The reaction is run at 63 °C for 45 min. After incubation, the colour changes from pink to yellow. Explain what the colour change signifies and why the assay is isothermal.
steps: LAMP uses Bst DNA polymerase with strand‑displacement activity, allowing amplification at a single temperature.
Pyrophosphate ions produced during DNA synthesis react with a metal‑ion indicator (e.g. calcein) causing a colour shift from pink (negative) to yellow (positive).
The colour change therefore indicates successful amplification of the target DNA.
worked.ans: Yellow colour = positive amplification; isothermal because strand‑displacing polymerase eliminates need for thermal cycling.
